architectural_implications.before: Production logging/APM and the offline eval harness are separate systems with an export-and-reformat step between them.
architectural_implications.consequence: The trace schema becomes a load-bearing interface; changing it changes both observability and the eval corpus, and any production event is a candidate test case with no manual curation.
architectural_implications.observation: Production traces and offline evaluation records are the same artifact type, handled by one observability system.

architectural_implications.after: wandb/core and WandBAgentFactory stay aligned via a four-hour sync job, so experiments run the shipped code path.
architectural_implications.before: Offline research happens in a sandbox or notebook that diverges from deployed code; promising results are reimplemented before shipping.
architectural_implications.consequence: No reimplementation gap, but research iteration velocity becomes coupled to production code structure and bounded by the sync window.
architectural_implications.observation: The research environment is the production codebase synced on a schedule, not a fork.

architectural_implications.after: Candidate variants are benchmarked against a baseline and land as code changes through review.
architectural_implications.before: Improvements are made as manual prompt/config edits deployed directly into the running agent.

architectural_implications.observation: The agent's improvement output is a PR into wandb/core gated on beating a baseline, not a live policy update.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Zubin Aysola
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Building and evaluating self-improving AI software agents using W&B Weave and CoreWeave ARIA.
  • Purpose: Explain the methodology of evaluating, tracing, and self-improving AI software agents by treating research and production code as identical. Zubin Aysola from Weights & Biases presents a deep dive into how they evaluate and build ARIA, their self-improving AI research and iteration agent. The talk covers the covariation between benchmarks, evaluations, and agent configuration, introducing W&B Weave as an observability and evaluation framework that enables a closed-loop flywheel where every production error or success becomes a test case and fix.

Topic Map

Introduction to Agent Harnesses and Evaluation

  • Explanation: Zubin introduces himself, his work at Weights & Biases on the ARIA agent, and the challenges of agentic harnesses across different benchmarks.
  • Key claims:
    • Benchmarks, evaluations, and agents are covariant; changing one affects all others.
    • Packaging agents with different tool calls and frameworks leads to varied benchmark performance.
  • Examples:
    • Terminal-Bench 2.0 scores comparing different agent harnesses across base models.
  • Terminology:
    • Agent Harness
    • Terminal-Bench 2.0
    • Covariance
  • Why it matters: Understanding how packaging and tooling affect agent performance is critical for reliable agent deployment.

Introducing W&B Weave and CoreWeave ARIA

  • Explanation: Overview of W&B Weave as an observability platform for agents and ARIA as a self-improving AI research agent.
  • Key claims:
    • Weave provides observability for both production and offline tracing.
    • ARIA uses offline hill-climbing to self-improve by running evaluations against codebases.
  • Examples:
    • Live demo showing ARIA analyzing production traces, writing evaluation tasks, and hill-climbing.
  • Terminology:
    • W&B Weave
    • ARIA
    • Observability platform
    • Hill-climbing
  • Why it matters: Unified observability bridges the gap between production logs and offline development sandboxes.

The Flywheel: Research and Production Are the Same Code

  • Explanation: Details on how the codebase between production and research remains identical through automated sync jobs.
  • Key claims:
    • Research and production code should be identical to prevent drift during iterative improvements.
    • A four-hour sync job keeps research and production environments aligned.
  • Examples:
    • wandb/core repository synced with WandBAgentFactory via scheduled jobs.
  • Terminology:
    • WandBAgentFactory
    • Sync job
    • Code drift
  • Why it matters: Eliminates code drift between what runs in production and what is tested offline.

The Execution Engine: Six Phases per Record

  • Explanation: Breaking down the evaluation architecture into distinct phases: Hydrate, Setup, Rehydrate, Run, Score, and Teardown.
  • Key claims:
  • Examples:
    • Execution pipeline showing run lane and setup lane running independently.
  • Terminology:
    • Hydrate
    • Setup
    • Rehydrate
    • Run
    • Score
    • Teardown
  • Why it matters: Structured execution phases enable reliable, parallelized evaluation of agent trajectories.

Key Points

Benchmarks and Agents Are Covariant

  • Explanation: Any change to the evaluation dataset, harness, or reward model impacts all other parts of the agent system.
  • Evidence: Observed differences in Terminal-Bench 2.0 scores across different harness configurations.
  • Practical implication: Engineers must measure agent performance in both production and offline simulation environments simultaneously.

Research and Production Code Unification

  • Explanation: Using identical codebases for production agents and offline research environments prevents drift.
  • Evidence:
  • Practical implication: Ensures that improvements discovered during offline research directly translate to production capabilities.

Every Production Miss Becomes a Test and a Fix

  • Explanation: Production errors are captured as traces, turned into evaluation tasks, and fed back into the agent iteration loop.
  • Evidence: ARIA live demo logging a production error trace and creating a new hill-climbing evaluation task.
  • Practical implication: Creates a continuous self-improvement flywheel without relying solely on manual prompt engineering.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

W&B Agent Flywheel

  • How it works: Production traces are logged via Weave, analyzed for failures, converted into evaluation tasks, benchmarked against candidate agent variants, and deployed via PR.
  • Components:
    • Production miss
    • Diagnose and propose
    • Iterate the candidate
    • Benchmark vs baseline
    • PR into wandb/core
  • When to use: When developing and scaling autonomous software engineering agents in production.

Agent Execution Engine Phases

  • How it works: Executes evaluation records through six discrete phases separated into independent lanes for running and setup.
  • Components:
    • Hydrate
    • Setup
    • Rehydrate
    • Run
    • Score
    • Teardown
  • When to use: When building robust simulation and offline evaluation harnesses for LLM agents.

Examples & Case Studies

ARIA encountered an attribute error in production due to an uncalled logging method.

  • Illustrates: How production errors are automatically captured and turned into evaluation tasks.
  • Lesson: Production failures provide the highest-fidelity test cases for agent self-improvement.

Zubin triggered ARIA live to take a production trace, log it into offline evaluations, and run candidate agent variants.

  • Illustrates: End-to-end closed-loop agent iteration using W&B Weave.
  • Lesson: Agents can autonomously diagnose their own SDK bugs and propose code fixes.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Use W&B Weave for unified agent observability across production and offline environments.
    • Structure evaluation pipelines into clear phases (Hydrate, Setup, Rehydrate, Run, Score, Teardown).
  • Strategic:
    • Treat research code and production code as the exact same codebase to eliminate drift.
    • Build a flywheel where every production failure becomes a benchmark test case.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do different tool-use call configurations impact agent success rates across diverse tasks?
    • What are the best practices for scaling parallel evaluation sandboxes cost-effectively?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Benchmarks, evaluations, and agents are covariant. (theoretical)
  • W&B Weave provides complete observability for both production and offline tracing of agents. (technical)

Notable Quotes

"Benchmarks, evaluations, and the agents and how you configure them are all covariant." "Every production miss becomes a test — then a fix."

Compressed Summary

  • Agents, benchmarks, and evaluations are covariant systems.
  • W&B Weave provides end-to-end observability for production and offline agent traces.
  • Research and production code share an identical codebase synced every four hours.
  • The evaluation engine operates across six phases: hydrate, setup, rehydrate, run, score, and teardown.
  • Production failures become automated evaluation tasks in a continuous self-improvement flywheel.
  • Keywords: agents, observability, evaluation, flywheel, tracing
  • Core insight: Synchronizing research and production codebases while feeding production failures back into automated evaluation loops creates a powerful self-improving agent flywheel.

- **Evidence**: Observed differences in Terminal-Bench 2.0 scores across different harness configurations.
- **Practical implication**: Engineers must measure agent performance in both production and offline simulation environments simultaneously.
### Research and Production Code Unification
- **Explanation**: Using identical codebases for production agents and offline research environments prevents drift.
- **Evidence**: 
- **Practical implication**: Ensures that improvements discovered during offline research directly translate to production capabilities.
### Every Production Miss Becomes a Test and a Fix
- **Explanation**: Production errors are captured as traces, turned into evaluation tasks, and fed back into the agent iteration loop.
- **Evidence**: ARIA live demo logging a production error trace and creating a new hill-climbing evaluation task.
- **Practical implication**: Creates a continuous self-improvement flywheel without relying solely on manual prompt engineering.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### W&B Agent Flywheel
- **How it works**: Production traces are logged via Weave, analyzed for failures, converted into evaluation tasks, benchmarked against candidate agent variants, and deployed via PR.
- **Components**:
  - Production miss
  - Diagnose and propose
  - Iterate the candidate
  - Benchmark vs baseline
  - PR into wandb/core
- **When to use**: When developing and scaling autonomous software engineering agents in production.
### Agent Execution Engine Phases
- **How it works**: Executes evaluation records through six discrete phases separated into independent lanes for running and setup.
- **Components**:
  - Hydrate
  - Setup
  - Rehydrate
  - Run
  - Score
  - Teardown
- **When to use**: When building robust simulation and offline evaluation harnesses for LLM agents.
